occupation: Marine Shore-Based Engineering and Management Technician
role: Marine Superintendent at a Ship Management Company (chief officer come ashore)
headline: Out of a Zhoushan fishing village, twelve years on ocean-going bulk carriers, four of them as chief officer, then ashore for the sake of a child: a marine superintendent at a ship management company on Shanghai's North Bund who watches the fleet-tracking screen by day and takes captains' satellite calls at midnight
unit: The marine department of a ship management company under a shipping group on Shanghai's North Bund (some thirty ocean-going bulk carriers)
unit_type: Ship management company under a state-owned shipping group
education: Bachelor's degree in navigation, holding a chief officer's certificate of competency
level: You know shipboard life with your eyes shut: loading, ballasting, lifeboats, fire drills, where a port state control officer looks first. But you haven't yet read through the shore-side management manuals, writing official letters, running internal audits and dealing with the maritime safety administration and the class society are all new, and sitting in an office watching ship positions, it always feels one layer removed.
intro: You grew up in a fishing village on Zhoushan, studied navigation, and spent twelve years on ocean-going bulk carriers, from cadet all the way to chief officer. The year your child was born you were at anchor off South America, and you saw the baby for the first time on a video call. Last year you came ashore and joined this ship management company on the North Bund. As of today you no longer stand on the bridge. You sit in front of a screen, keeping watch, on behalf of the people on a dozen ships, over the things they cannot see.
salary_note: Estimate: marine posts at Shanghai ship management companies are paid on the shore scale, a little over ten percent above the national average, with an annuity. But compared with a chief officer's dollar wages at sea, your first year ashore brought in less than half. In years when freight rates are good, the year-end bonus is bigger.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Boarding a ship to carry out an internal audit of the safety management system

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Taking a watch and running a position check on the whole fleet

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 15 related listings nationwide, 1 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: You take the metro to the North Bund, and coming out of the station you see a tug on the Huangpu pushing a barge downstream. Out of habit you glance at its draft before walking into the office tower.

You open the fleet-tracking platform and check your fourteen ships one by one. One has made a detour outside the Taiwan Strait. You pull up the captain's noon report from last night: a typhoon ahead, and he's steering clear.

At the morning meeting, technical, marine and crewing sit at one table. The technical manager says one ship's main engine exhaust temperatures are running high and it'll be checked when it bunkers in Singapore; crewing says three ships need crew changes next month and the visas are still stuck.

You video-call the captain of a ship approaching Port Hedland in Australia and go through the port state control self-check list item by item: lifeboat release gear, emergency fire pump, the oily water separator record book. The captain says it's all in order. You have him send photos of the record book and read them page by page.

Another ship sends in a hot-work application for the engine room, to replace a stretch of pipe at anchor. You check the gas testing, the isolation and the fire watch arrangements, write your comments in the review box and pass it to your manager to sign.
Downstairs at lunch you run into a classmate you sailed with, still a chief officer, home on leave this trip. He asks how life ashore is. You say half the money, and you get to go home at night.

The International Maritime Organization has issued another circular, and you revise a procedure in the company's safety management manual against the English original, checking three handbooks for every sentence.

Your child has just fallen asleep when the phone rings: the captain of the ship dodging the typhoon, on the satellite phone. The track has shifted and he wants to anchor off Zhoushan. Listening, you open your laptop and wake your manager too.

ladder.title: Safety / Marine / Technical Assistant
ladder.focus: Organize management system documents, sit shore-side watches, help with shipboard inspections and file repair orders, and learn the regulations and the company's fleet. You move up by mastering the management system and English maritime paperwork.

ladder.title: Marine Superintendent / Technical Superintendent
ladder.focus: Own the management system monitoring, risk assessments, port state control preparation or maintenance plan reviews for several ships on your own. Promotion comes from sea time or a senior officer's certificate.

ladder.title: Marine Manager / Technical Manager
ladder.focus: Oversee the fleet's safety and pollution prevention or technical condition, guide masters and crews, approve high-risk work and repairs, and plan internal and external audits. Requires a master's or chief engineer's certificate and real sea time in that rank.

ladder.title: Head of Safety and Quality / Designated Person Ashore (DPA)
ladder.focus: As the company's designated person, report directly to top management and answer for the management system's effectiveness, accident investigations and emergency command. Promotion to senior management comes from the fleet's overall safety record and management ability.

ladder.title: Technical Director / General Manager, Ship Management Company
ladder.focus: Run the fleet's operations, technical affairs, safety and costs, answering to shipowners and customers.

ai_tasks.name: Taking a watch and running a position check on the whole fleet
ai_tasks.how: AI pulls AIS and ship reports automatically, compares each vessel against its planned route and speed and flags deviations. A person only needs to look at the flags, spot-check, and decide whether to call the captain.

ai_tasks.name: Approving a hot-work application for an engine room
ai_tasks.how: AI can check whether the application is complete, whether the work area and risk controls follow procedure, and point out what's missing. A person has to judge whether conditions on board can really keep it safe, and sign for the approval.

ai_tasks.name: Taking a ship through a port state control self-check before arrival
ai_tasks.how: AI generates a self-check list from the checklists and that port's history of deficiencies, and collects the issues and photos the ship reports. A person has to judge how serious each deficiency is, make sure the ship actually fixes it, and talk the priorities through with the captain.

ai_tasks.name: Running a voyage risk assessment and issuing a risk notice
ai_tasks.how: AI gathers weather, routing, piracy and accident information and drafts a risk list and notice. A person has to weigh it against the ship's condition, the crew's state and what the company can bear, decide whether to reroute or carry on, and lead the ship-shore discussion.

ai_tasks.name: Boarding a ship to carry out an internal audit of the safety management system
ai_tasks.how: AI can help prepare the audit checklist, sort past non-conformities and draft the report. But boarding to look, interviewing the crew, judging whether the system really works and pointing out problems face to face rests mainly on people.

ai_tasks.name: Standing by a dry-docking at the shipyard and signing it off
ai_tasks.how: AI can help draft the repair specification, compare quotes and track progress. But staying at the yard to watch quality, negotiating on the spot with the shipyard, verifying the work and signing for acceptance need a person there, answering for it.

ai_tasks.name: Launching a ship-shore emergency response to a late-night report of engine-room flooding
ai_tasks.how: Once the report comes in, AI can pull up the emergency plan, the call list and the ship's particulars, keep the timeline and draft external notifications. A person has to judge the danger on incomplete information, direct the response, contact salvage and the managers, and carry the responsibility for the decisions.

events.e_detained: One of your ships is detained by port state control in Australia: the oily water separator records don't add up, and it's held three days in port. You barely sleep three nights running, calling the captain, the agent and the class society round after round, and on the fourth day the ship is released.
events.e_zero: An old ship whose repairs you'd been chasing for three months passes inspection in a Japanese port with zero deficiencies. The captain sends a photo of the inspection report followed by a thumbs-up, and you forward it to the department group.
events.e_typhoon_night: One night in typhoon season, three of your ships are on the edge of the storm's track. You and your manager keep watch in the office all night, calling each captain in turn: alter course, anchor, double up the moorings. By daybreak all three have reported safe.
events.e_ais_ai: The watch system now pulls AIS and ship reports automatically, compares each against its planned route and speed, and marks deviations in red. A position check that used to take you an hour a watch now means looking only at the red ones and deciding whether to call the captain.
events.e_ai_miss: The AI-compiled voyage risk notice is thorough: weather, piracy, port congestion. What it doesn't notice is that the crew on that ship have been aboard ten months straight. You add a line at the end, call crewing, and get two people relieved early.
events.e_flooding: At three in the morning a ship reports flooding in the engine room. The emergency system pulls up the plan and the call list automatically, but the captain's voice on the phone is tight. You ask him item by item about the water level, the pumps, the list, while a colleague contacts the nearest port and salvage. By daybreak the leak is plugged.
events.e_pay_cut: Your first year-end bonus ashore arrives, and when you add it up, the year's income is less than half what you made as chief officer. Your spouse says less money, but you're home. You nod, and push the plan to pay off the mortgage early back by two years.
events.e_spring: For the first time in twelve years you spend Spring Festival at home. On New Year's Eve you make dumplings, and yours keep falling over. Your child laughs at you; you say that on the ship, the cook made them.
events.e_land_sway: For the first few months ashore, lying in bed at night you still feel yourself rocking gently, like a ship in a swell. Your spouse says you reach out for the edge of the bed in your sleep.
events.e_parents_meeting: You go to your child's parent-teacher meeting for the first time. When the teacher reads out your child's name, she says his essay was titled My Father at Sea. You sit on the little chair and don't dare look up.
events.e_drydock: A ship goes into dry dock at a Zhoushan shipyard and the technical manager can't cover it all, so you stand by at the yard for two weeks. Every day you're under the hull in the dock watching blasting and plate renewal and arguing with the yard about the schedule, and at night in the hotel you go through the repair list item by item.
events.e_doc_audit: The maritime safety administration comes to audit the company's management system, and the auditor samples the risk assessments and internal audit reports for your ships. You answer questions all morning, and at the end he writes zero non-conformities.
events.e_cii: Under the new carbon intensity rules, one of your old ships drops to a D rating. You, the technical team and the captain spend six months working out speeds and routes and recoat the hull bottom, and the next year the rating is back to C.
events.e_market_down: Bulk freight rates fall to their lowest in years. The company sells five old ships in one go and the department lets two people go. You stay, but there's no year-end bonus, and the ships under you go from fourteen to eighteen.
events.e_market_up: Freight rates triple in a year, and ship after ship sails fully loaded. At year's end the company pays a bonus like none you've ever seen, and you have your parents' house back home on Zhoushan rebuilt.
events.e_insomnia: The phone is on twenty-four hours a day, and you wake the moment it rings at night. In time, even on nights with no call, you wake at three and lie listening to the traffic outside, waiting for daylight.
events.e_foreign_crew: The company starts hiring foreign crew, and one ship has Chinese, Burmese and Filipino accents aboard. On an inspection you find the safety instructions are only in Chinese, and you stay up all night making a version in three languages.
events.e_father: Your father is in the hospital on Zhoushan. You go back Friday nights and return to Shanghai Sunday nights, two months running. The ward window looks out on the port, and he says that ship's sitting deep. You say yes, fully laden.
events.e_cadet: A third officer just starting out comes in on leave to do paperwork and stops you in the corridor to ask why you came ashore, and whether he should sail a few more years. You think a while and say: sail until you're chief officer. By then you'll know.
events.e_captain_friend: The captain you served under as chief officer retires, and when his last voyage ends in Shanghai you go to the quay to meet him. He doesn't look back as he comes down the gangway. He walks up to you and presses an old pair of binoculars into your hands.
events.e_remote: The company trials a smart ship, and from ashore you can see every reading in its engine room and every screen on its bridge. The young engineers say ships will need fewer people one day. Watching that ship on the screen, you think of all those three a.m. watches when you were alone on the bridge.
events.e_back: Twelve years standing at sea and over ten sitting ashore, and your back finally gives out. You switch to a standing desk, and when you take satellite calls you pace back and forth across the office, the way you did on the bridge.

c_master.title: Two years back at sea as captain, to go for Marine Manager
c_master.situation: The department is promoting a Marine Manager, and the requirement is a master's certificate and real sea time as captain. You only have a chief officer's certificate. The company is willing to send you back to sea as captain for two years, and once your time is in, bring you back as Marine Manager. But it means eight or nine months away at a stretch again, just as your child starts primary school.

options.label: Go back to sea as captain
options.result: In the captain's cabin you sign your first entry in the log book, and for the first time feel the weight of the whole ship on your shoulders. In two years you go home twice. Your child is taller each time, and the second time is a little shy of you.

options.label: Stay ashore
options.result: You say your child comes first. The manager's post goes to an old captain just off a ship. He asks you about every shore-side rule, and you ask him about everything new at sea.

c_ism.title: Sit for ISM/NSM internal auditor and registered safety engineer
c_ism.situation: Ashore, you don't get by on sea time alone; you also need the management system and safety credentials: ISM/NSM internal auditor, registered safety engineer. The safety engineer exam means working through four textbooks, and you've been away from textbooks for over a decade. In the evenings, when your child does homework, you sit beside him and do yours.

options.label: Take both
options.result: You pass internal auditor first time; the safety engineer exam takes two years. The day the certificate arrives, your child sticks his school award and your certificate side by side on the fridge.

options.label: Only internal auditor
options.result: You get the internal auditor qualification, and the first time you lead an audit team aboard, you turn up three old problems nobody had noticed. The safety engineer books you bought stay on the shelf.

c_detention.title: How to write the detention report
c_detention.situation: A ship has been detained by port state control and the company wants your root-cause analysis. The captain says spare parts that should have been approved ashore six months ago never were; the technical side says the ship simply didn't fill in its record book. Your report goes straight to the general manager's desk.

options.label: Write it straight; the shore shares the blame
options.result: You write that the spare-parts approval was held up six months, and that the record book wasn't filled in. The technical manager doesn't say hello to you in the corridor for days, and from then on the captains call you first when something comes up.

options.label: Focus on the ship's corrective actions
options.result: You write the report as the ship's corrective action plan, every item with a deadline. The general manager approves it. You take up the spare parts privately with the technical manager, and next month they're approved.

c_ai.title: Design the ship-shore watch process for working with AI
c_ai.situation: The company has installed an intelligent watch and emergency system, but nobody has said who calls when the AI flags something red, or who catches what it doesn't flag. The department wants someone who has sailed to define the ship-shore watch and emergency procedures. The work is messy, with meetings with the IT department every day.

options.label: Take it and define the process
options.result: The first rule you write is: for every ship, within any twenty-four hours, at least one person must speak to the captain in their own voice. The IT people say that's not a technical issue. You say that's exactly what it is.

options.label: Decline and keep your own ships
options.result: You say you're used to checking positions yourself. The IT department writes the procedures later, and at the review you add a few rules: what to do when the satellite link drops, what to do when the captain doesn't pick up.

c_singapore.title: A foreign ship manager in Singapore comes headhunting
c_singapore.situation: A foreign ship management company in Singapore is hiring a Marine Manager for a chemical tanker fleet, at more than double your current pay, working in English, with the whole family able to move. But your parents are on Zhoushan, your child is enrolled at school in Shanghai, and everything would start from scratch.

options.label: Move the family to Singapore
options.result: From your office in Singapore you can see hundreds of ships in the anchorage. Your English emails are slow at first; three months in, you no longer draft in your head before speaking in meetings. Your child learns English with a Singapore lilt.

options.label: Stay in Shanghai
options.result: You don't go. On weekends you take your child back to Zhoushan to see your parents, and on the seawall you point out the distant anchorage and teach him which ships are in ballast and which are laden.

c_surveyor.title: A class society wants you as a surveyor
c_surveyor.situation: A class society in Shanghai is hiring ship surveyors and likes that you have twelve years at sea and know management systems ashore. A surveyor boards ships to inspect and certify them, speaks as an independent third party, keeps more regular hours, and never gets captains' calls at midnight. But it means leaving the shipping company.

options.label: Become a surveyor
options.result: You hand the department back the work phone that was on twenty-four hours a day, and write the names of your fourteen ships in the handover book one last time.
options.end: You work as a class surveyor for many years, boarding hundreds of ships to inspect their lifeboats, hatch covers and anchor chains. Whenever you stand on the deck of an old ship, you look up at the bridge first and think of where you stood as chief officer.

options.label: Stay at the shipping company
options.result: You turn them down. That night a captain calls to say a gale has come up at the anchorage, and you go through it with him step by step on the phone, just as you once did on the bridge.

c_dpa.title: Apply for Head of Safety and Quality / Designated Person Ashore (DPA)
c_dpa.situation: The company's Designated Person Ashore is retiring. The post reports directly to top management and answers for whether the management system works, who investigates accidents and who commands emergencies. Anyone aboard any ship can bypass everyone else and call the DPA directly. If you get it, your phone can never be switched off again.

options.label: Apply
options.result: At the interview you don't recite the management system clauses. You talk about that three a.m. call about engine-room flooding, and the three things you changed afterward. The general manager asks if you're afraid. You say yes, which is why it has to be done.

options.label: Stay as Marine Manager
options.result: You recommend an old captain from another company. Whenever the new DPA isn't sure about something, his first call is still to you.

c_consult.title: A friend wants you in maritime safety consulting
c_consult.situation: An old classmate who sailed has started a maritime safety consultancy, writing management systems, running port state control training and doing internal audits for small and mid-sized shipowners, and he wants you as a partner. Your time would be your own and pay would depend on projects, no longer answering for the fate of a fleet. But you'd never have ships of your own again.

options.label: Go into consulting
options.result: On the day you resign, you put the binoculars the old captain gave you into your bag.
options.end: You work many years in maritime safety consulting, writing management systems and preparing inspections for dozens of shipowners. What you tell captains most often is: the first thing a port state control officer looks at when he boards is your people, not your paperwork.

options.label: Stay at the shipping company
options.result: You say you still want to look after your own ships. Your classmate later wins a training contract with your company, and when he comes to teach, he has the trainees all address you as Captain.

c_gm.title: Go for Technical Director / General Manager of the ship management company
c_gm.situation: The group is choosing a Technical Director / General Manager for the ship management company, to run the whole fleet's operations, technical affairs, safety and costs, answering to shipowners and customers. It means dealing with the group, banks, charterers and shipyards, and every yuan spent on repairs and every accident finding ends up on you.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: At your defense you bring out a decade and more of detentions, accidents and near misses, a line that falls year after year. A group leader asks what you'd do first. You say: make sure every ship has a satellite phone that actually gets through.

options.label: Don't apply; hold the safety line
options.result: You say you're better suited to the safety side. The new general manager comes from the commercial side, and every decision touching safety has to get past you first.

endings.retire: On your last day you hand the handover book for your dozen-odd ships to your successor and go through each ship's temper: which one has an old main engine, which captain likes to push his luck, which one's hatch covers leak. When you leave work, fog has come up over the river at the North Bund, and a ship heading downstream sounds a long blast on its horn. You stand by the river until it's done before you go.
endings.burnout: At that year's health check the doctor looks at your sleep records and blood pressure and tells you to stop keeping your phone on twenty-four hours a day. You step back from the department to sort records and go home on time every day. Now and then you still wake at night. You lie and listen a while; there's no call, and you fall back asleep.

stages: You own the management system monitoring for a dozen-odd ships on your own: checking positions and reading ship reports every day, taking ships due in port through port state control self-checks, reviewing applications for hot work and enclosed-space entry, and dealing with agents, the class society and the maritime administration on the captains' behalf. When the satellite phone rings at midnight, you're the first to answer; but the final signature on an approval is your manager's.

You oversee safety and pollution prevention across the whole fleet: guiding masters and crews, approving high-risk work and repair plans, planning the year's internal and external audits. You board ships to inspect them and sit in the captain's cabin talking about his crew, and back ashore you sign your own name on high-risk work permits. When there's an accident or a near miss, you're the first on scene or the first to decide.

You are the company's Designated Person Ashore, and anyone on any ship can bypass everyone and call you directly. You report to top management and answer for whether the system works, how accidents are investigated and how emergencies are commanded. When something goes wrong, you sit in the emergency command room listening to the captain while deciding whether to call salvage and whether to notify the authorities.

You run the whole fleet's operations, technical affairs, safety and costs: whether to buy new ships, whether to repair or sell old ones, how to deal with charterers and banks. You answer to the group and the shipowners, and at board meetings you talk about the fleet's accounts and its accident rate. Every year you still pick one ship to board, and stand on its bridge for an hour.
work: A ship nearing Qingdao reports that a lifeboat release hook is sticking. You dig out its maintenance record from six months ago, have the crew do a trial release by the procedure and send you video, and only once you're satisfied do you let it come in for inspection.

Zhou from crewing says a second officer has a family emergency and needs to sign off early. You map out that ship's operations for its next two ports and agree with the captain how to split the watches before writing yes on the crew change request.

Doing a voyage risk assessment for a ship about to transit the Gulf of Aden, you mark every piracy incident in the area that year on the chart, then have the captain send photos of the protective measures and check them one by one.

You board a newly acquired second-hand ship for inspection and don't look at the paperwork first. You spend an hour walking the engine room and end up with twenty-odd entries in the superintendent's log, the first being that the fire pump valves have been painted shut.

A ship needs to enter a cargo hold at anchor for enclosed-space work. You add a condition to the permit: test the air again after four hours of ventilation, with the chief officer photographing the readings and sending them to you. Only after seeing them do you sign.

On the annual internal audit you take two young superintendents aboard five ships. On one, you ask a seaman to show you on the spot how to close a fuel tank vent. He searches for three minutes and can't find it. You note it in the report, and don't scold him.

A ship sideswipes a fishing boat off the mouth of the Yangtze. At midnight you take your seat in the emergency command room and ask first whether anyone is in the water, then about the hull, and only then have a colleague draft the report to the maritime administration.
A young captain calls you privately to say the company's schedules are too tight and he's afraid to say so. You never tell anyone who called, and next month's voyage plan has an extra day of slack.

At an accident inquiry, everyone wants to call a flooded cargo hold human error. You spread out three years of hatch cover maintenance records and insist that the shore-side maintenance plan go into the root causes too.

The group wants to buy five more second-hand ships to grow the fleet. You read every one's survey reports and inspection records and strike out two, with the reason on the first page: the money for these two ships will all go on repairs.

A major charterer comes to discuss a three-year contract of affreightment, and the last thing they ask about is your safety record. You have ten years of detention rates put up on the screen, and they sign on the spot.

In the annual budget you add a line for crew communications on every ship. Finance says it isn't a necessary expense. You say that people at sea being able to talk to their families often does more good than any inspection.
past: You grow up in a fishing village on Zhoushan, where your father is a fisherman. The summer after middle school he takes you out to sea once. You're sick all day, and afterward, of all things, you go down to the wharf every day to watch the big ships come in.

For the gaokao (college entrance exam) you apply for navigation at a maritime university. Your mother says life at sea is hard, your father says it pays well, and what you think is that you could go see the places those big ships go.
After graduating you join a Capesize bulk carrier as a deck cadet. Your first voyage is to Brazil, more than forty days, and standing your first night watch on the bridge you see the southern stars.

You get your second officer's certificate and take charge of the navigation equipment and charts. On those night watches in the Singapore Strait, ships nose to tail, you alter course dozens of times a night, and come off watch with sweat in your palms.

You make chief officer, in charge of loading, ballast and the whole deck. At your first inspection in Australia, the port state control officer goes over your lifeboats for forty minutes and in the end says one word: good.

The day your child is born you are at anchor off South America, the satellite connection on and off. You see the baby's face for the first time on a video call, the picture freezes, and you stare at that frozen face for a long time.

When your contract ends you sign off and spend two months at home, just as your child learns to say Daddy. You interview for a marine superintendent job at this company on the North Bund. The interviewer asks why you're coming ashore. You say you want to hear your child say it a few more times.

late.pension_note: Estimate: the state-owned shipping group paid full pension contributions on actual wages, including all those years at sea, plus a company annuity. Together they come to a little over half your last monthly pay.
scenes: In your first week of retirement you still wake in the night and reach for the phone on the nightstand. The screen is blank. You check the forecast: strong winds over the East China Sea. You wonder which ships are out there.

The maritime university invites you back to talk to the students. You don't talk about management system clauses. You talk about that three a.m. engine-room flooding, and when you get to the captain's voice going tight, the classroom is very quiet.
You go back to your hometown on Zhoushan and buy a little sampan by the wharf, rowing out to fish on fine days. You still read the sky, the tide and the wind before casting off.
Your grandchild asks what it's like at sea. You dig the old binoculars out of a trunk and stand with him on the seawall looking at the distant anchorage, counting the ships one by one.
In the first months after you step back, you lock the work phone in a drawer, but every night at ten your hand still goes to your pocket without thinking.
At last you can sleep through the night, and your blood pressure comes down. In the mornings you walk along the Huangpu and turn back where you can see the mouth of the river at Wusong.
On the day you file your retirement papers, the young people in the department give you a model of the ship you served on as chief officer. You set it on the bookshelf beside the binoculars.
In your first year away from the shipping company, whenever a typhoon warning goes out you still open the ship-tracking website to see where those dozen-odd ships are.
At Yangshan port you come across a ship you once managed, its hull freshly painted, its name unchanged. You stand on the quay looking at it a long time. Nobody aboard knows you.

A young superintendent you trained has become the DPA. He sends you a photo: the first line of the company's ship-shore watch procedure is still the one about someone speaking to every captain every day.
Your child is applying to university. You say nothing and watch what goes on the application form. It isn't navigation. You let out a breath, and feel something else you can't quite name.
In an old trunk you find your first log book. On the first page is an entry you copied as a cadet: weather fine, wind southeast force four, moderate swell, vessel proceeding normally.

closing.retire: Many years later, one evening, you sit on the seawall back home on Zhoushan as the ships in the distant anchorage light up one by one. You lift the old binoculars and look a while. None of them are yours now, but you still look at each in turn, making sure they're all riding steady at anchor.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you are watering plants on the balcony when a long blast of a ship's horn comes up from the Huangpu below. You stop and listen until it ends, then go on to the next pot.
closing.end: Many years later, in a drawer, you find the work phone long since retired. It won't switch on. You weigh it in your hand, remember all those rings in the middle of the night, and put it back where it was.
